attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite name and tile in the [place sprite on top of random tile] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How many fish sprites appear on the screen when you press play? 

❓Why do 8 fish sprites appear on the screen, when there are only two [set sprite to] blocks?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 By placing a block in a [repeat] loop, it causes the code to run the number of times specified in the parameter. In this case, the [repeat] loop sets and places two different sprites, four times in a row, creating 8 sprites on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Place multiple fish sprites on the screen!


Open Loops and drag a [repeat] loop inside the [on start] container after the [set tilemap to] block. Drag both [set sprite to] blocks inside the [repeat] loop.


Add a [place sprite on top of random tile] block inside the [repeat] loop. Select the (fishSprite) variable name and the light blue tile.


Click ▶ to see the loop create multiple fish that will now appear on the screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you separate the [set sprite to] code blocks, one into each conditional opening, and change the <% chance> they appear?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How is using the (pick random) block in the [repeat] loop similar and different than how you’ve added randomization to projects before?

❓What would you change to have more orange fish sprites appear? More blue fish sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 While clicking on an individual block, the ninja can press Ctrl to move a single block (without also moving the blocks below/attached to it). This may be useful as they are adding and rearranging the blocks within the [if then] conditional.

💡Remind the ninja that the value in the <% chance> value block designates how likely (out of 100) that a block will run. In this case, 40% of the time (4 times out of 10), an orange fish sprite will appear. If a ninja wants to increase the number of orange sprites, they can increase the value in the <% chance> block closer to 100.
steps.instructions:
Randomize the color and number of fish that appear! 


Open Math and drag a (pick random) value block into the parameter of the [repeat] loop. Type the minimum and maximum number of sprites that could appear on screen. 


Open Logic and drag an [if then else] conditional inside the top of the [repeat] loop. Drag one [set sprite to] block inside the [then] opening and the other [set sprite to] block inside the [else] opening.


Open Math and drag out a <% chance> value block. Replace the conditional’s <true> value with the <% chance> value block. Change the number to a percentage value between 0 and 100 to set how likely the first sprite will appear.


Click ▶ to see the number of Orange and Blue sprites change each time the project runs!

steps.hints: ❓ Does your [repeat] loop appear after the [set list to] code block, and repeat 4 times to set and place each image in the (seaweedList)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How many seaweed sprites should appear on the screen? How many seaweed sprites can you actually see?

❓What happens if you change the parameter in the [repeat] loop to 3? What happens if you change it to 5?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In order to ensure that all 4 seaweed sprites appear on the screen, the [repeat] loop parameter needs to match the number of values in the array. If the loop repeats more times than there are values in the array, it will cause an error in the code.

💡All 4 seaweed sprites will not visually appear to be on the screen because they are all being placed in the same position.
steps.instructions:
Add seaweed along the bottom to add challenge to the game. 


Add a [repeat] loop to the bottom of the [on start] container. Drag a [set sprite to] block inside the [repeat] loop, name the variable (seaweedSprite) and select Seaweed as the sprite kind. There is already an array of seaweed images in the starter code, so open Arrays then drag a (get and remove first value from (list)) value block into the sprite image bubble and select (seaweedList) as the array. 


Drag a [place sprite on top of] block into the [repeat] loop, select the sprite name, then set the row parameter to 5 so the seaweed sprites appear along the bottom.


There are 4 seaweed images in the array, so keep the loop set to repeat 4 times, once for each image in the array.


Click ▶ to see the seaweed images appear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place a (columnNumber) variable within the [place sprite on top of] row parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does using a [set variable to] and [change [variable] by] block fix this bug?

❓ What does the variable represent in the [set variable to] block? What changes in the [place sprite on top of] block, after the variable is updated?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Make sure the Ninja has placed the [set [variable] to] block above the [repeat] loop, so that the variable is set before it is assigned and changed inside the loop.

💡By placing the [change [variable] by] block inside the [repeat] loop, each time the loop runs, it increases the sprite’s column value and moves the sprite two tiles to the right. This places all 4 Seaweed sprites in different positions, where they are able to be viewed on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The seaweed sprites all appeared in the same column of the tilemap. Use a variable to change the column number for each of the 4 seaweed sprites.


Open Variables and drag a [set [variable] to] block inside the [on start] container, above the seaweedSprite [repeat] loop, to create a new variable named [columnNumber]. Set the variable to 1. Drag a (columnNumber) variable into the col parameter in the [place sprite on top of] block.


Open Variables and drag a [change [variable] by] block inside the [repeat] loop, below the [place sprite on top of] block, to change the (columnNumber) variable by 2 every time the code repeats.


Click ▶ to see the 4 seaweed images appear in different columns along the bottom!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you go to the Variables code menu to “Make a Variable” called “question”, then use a [set variable to] block to set the “question” variable [on countdown end]?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you think the [question] variable will be used?

❓ How might you use user input to update what is stored in the [question] variable?

❓ What else could happen when the countdown ends? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to recall skills learned in the previous level of asking for user input and using that response to trigger an event in the project. Prompt the ninja to think about how they might use the [question] variable to store user input in this project.
steps.instructions:
Add a timed element to the game! 


Drag a [start countdown] block into the [on start] container. Set the parameter to 4 seconds. 


Drag out an [on countdown end] container then drag a [set [variable] to] block inside the container to create a [question] variable. 


Use a (pick random) value block to select a random number between 0 to 2 as the value of the (question) variable.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you duplicate the <(question) = 0> block, then update the right parameter to 1 in the [else if] condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What question might be asked when the variable equals 0?

❓What question might be asked when the variable equals 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Help the ninja with the placement of each value block, reminding them of the importance of sequence. Encourage the ninja to double check that each value block is inside of the correct parameter.
steps.instructions:
Ask the player a question about how many fish they remember seeing when the countdown ends!  


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on countdown end] container. Click + on the conditional 2 times to add an [else if] condition.


Replace <true> with a <0=0> comparison block and fill the left parameter with a (question) bubble. The right parameter should be set to 0. 


Right click to duplicate the entire <question = 0> block and insert it into the [else if] value, then update the right parameter to 1.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag a <0=0> comparison block into the [game over] toggle and update the parameters with the question and max length?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What question will be asked when the variable equals 0?

❓What question will be asked when the variable equals 1? 

❓How might the project check to see whether the user’s response is correct? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the Ninja to review their code to ensure that if the question variable is equal to 0, the user will be asked about how many orange fish are on screen, and if the question variable is equal to 1, the user will be asked about how many blue fish are on screen. Ask the ninja what might happen when the question variable is equal to 2.

💡Help the ninja with the placement of each value blocks, reminding them of the importance of sequence. Encourage the ninja to double check that each value block is inside of the correct parameter.
steps.instructions:
Match the question asked with the number stored by the [question] variable!


Drag a [game over] block into the [then] opening of the [if] condition. Replace the <WIN> toggle with another <0=0> comparison block.


Open Game and drag an <ask for number> value block into the left bubble of the <0=0> comparison block. Type “How many orange fish?” in the parameter, then click the + to set the max length as 2 digits.


Duplicate the [game over] block to insert it into the [else if] opening; update the text to “blue” fish.

steps.hints: ❓ Does the sprite kind in the (array of sprites of kind) match the color mentioned in that [game over] block’s question?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓How does the project check to see if the user’s response matches the number of Fish sprites on the screen?

❓What else might happen if the user answers correctly or incorrectly?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide the ninja to understand that the <0=0> comparison block is comparing the user’s response to the length of the Orange or Blue fish sprite array. This value is determined by the (pick random) block in the [repeat] loop, dictating how many fish of a certain kind appear on the screen.
steps.instructions:
Check the player’s answer by comparing the user response to the length of the array of Orange or Blue fish. 


From Arrays, drag out a (length of array) value block, then place it into the right parameter of the <0 = 0> comparison block, inside the [if] condition. 


Open Sprites and drag an (array of sprites of kind) value block into the space where the (list) bubble is. Delete (list) as needed. Select the Orange sprite kind.


Duplicate the entire (length of array (array of sprites of kind)) value block, then place it into the right parameter of the <0 = 0> comparison block, inside the [else if] condition. Change the sprite kind to Blue.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you duplicate a [game over] block into the [else] opening, and use a (0 + 0) operator to add together the lengths of the two arrays?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project find the total number of Fish sprites that appear on the screen?

❓ What other questions could you add to this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡The ninja will need to either delete the existing (length of array (array of sprites of kind)) value block inside the <0 = 0> comparison block, or move it to a different location in the editor. They should then place the (0 + 0) operator inside the right parameter of the  <0 = 0> comparison block. Once placed, the (length of array (array of sprites of kind)) value block can be readded.

💡Encourage the ninja to think about the similarities between the (0 + 0) operator and the <0 = 0> comparison block and how their uses might be different. Guide the ninja to notice the shape of each block and how that might impact where each block fits within the code.
steps.instructions:
Add one additional question that asks the player the total number of orange and blue fish!


Duplicate the [game over] block again and place it into the [else] opening. Update the question to say “How many total fish?”


Open Math and drag a (0 + 0) operator into the right parameter of the <0 = 0> comparison block. Duplicate the entire (length of array) for the Blue sprite kind, then drag it into one of the openings in the (0 + 0) operator. Duplicate the entire (length of array) for the Orange sprite kind, then drag it into the other opening.


Click ▶ to see 1 of the 3 questions appear when time is up! Play several times until you see the 3 different questions appear!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add customizations to your project, such as animations, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓What type of animation or screen effects might you add to this project?

❓ What directions will help people understand how this project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project by adding movement animation to the fish sprites and adding game directions with a splash screen!


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Memory Game
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses repeat loops and conditionals to test a game player’s memory!

validationItems.text: Use a loop to create multiple fish sprites.
Randomize the number and color of fish sprites that appear on screen.
Use a loop and a variable to create 4 seaweed sprites from an array of images and place them on screen.
Use a countdown timer to pick a random question after the timer ends.
Ask the player about the number of blue OR orange fish on screen, depending on the question number randomly selected.
Ask the player a question about the total number of blue AND orange fish on screen.
Customize the project with sprite animations and game directions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Orange Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about repeat and for loops. A loop is a chunk of code that repeats until a specific condition is met. You’ll use what you already know about variables and arrays to create loops that respond to specific conditions. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level #4:

badges.title: Deja Vu
badges.description: Use different types of loops to repeat code in a project.

badges.title: Once More, With Feeling
badges.description: Use a repeat loop to repeat code a given number of times.

badges.title: Yearbook
badges.description: Create and use an array of sprites.

badges.title: Roll Call
badges.description: Use a for element of loop to make something happen to each item in an array.

badges.title: Freeze Tag
badges.description: Use a pause in a project.

badges.title: Button Down
badges.description: Check if a button is being pressed before making something happen in a project.
